mentors.name: Cat Wu
mentors.role: Founding engineer and product lead, Claude Code
mentors.bio: Co-built Claude Code from the first internal prototype and shaped it into a product used far beyond engineering. Talks about the workflows Anthropic's own engineers discovered: slash commands for feature development and first-pass code review, subagents for narrow jobs.
ideas: Let Claude be the product manager first: ask what you want, write the spec, then the plan, then the to-do list.
Automate the first pass of code review; keep a human on the merge.
Non-technical users find uses the team never imagined; design for that.
mentors.deep: Anthropic runs a /code-review command on every pull request internally, and a /feature-dev command that forces the spec-plan-todo sequence. The lesson for a non-engineer is that the sequence matters more than the code: the agent is much better at executing a plan it helped write than at guessing what you meant.
src: How to use Claude Code like the people who built it (Every, with Cat Wu and Boris Cherny)
mentors.ask: What do the non-engineers at Anthropic use it for?

dialogue.you: Who reviews what the agent wrote?
dialogue.m: A slash command does the first pass on every pull request inside Anthropic. A person still approves the merge.

dialogue.you: Where do I start when I do not know the code?
dialogue.m: With the sequence the team's feature command forces: ask what is actually wanted, build the specification, then a detailed plan, then a to-do list.
That is the design goal. They work to lower the barrier for people who are not: it should be intuitive enough that you drop in and it works, with point-and-click surfaces next to the terminal.

exercise.title: Spec, plan, to-do, in that order
steps: Pick one small thing you want built this week.
Write workspace/mentors/wu/spec.md with three headings: ## Spec, ## Plan, ## To-do.
Under Spec say what done looks like; under Plan the steps; under To-do the list you would hand an agent.
Add notes.md with ## What I learned.
exercise.done: spec.md has a Spec, a Plan and a To-do section

mentors.name: Andrej Karpathy
mentors.role: Researcher, educator; ex OpenAI, ex Tesla AI
mentors.bio: Founding member of OpenAI, led Tesla Autopilot's AI team, taught Stanford's first deep-learning class, and now teaches the internet: the Zero to Hero series builds neural networks from scratch in code, and the general-audience talks explain LLMs without maths. Coined "vibe coding" in 2025 and "Software 3.0" for programming in natural language.
ideas: Build the smallest version yourself; understanding follows from code you can run.
LLMs are a new kind of computer: the prompt is the program.
Vibe coding is real and fine for the right projects; know when you are doing it.
mentors.deep: Zero to Hero goes micrograd (a 100-line autograd engine), makemore (character-level language models, five parts), a WaveNet, then a GPT built to the 2017 paper, then the tokenizer. The general-audience track covers how LLMs are trained and how he uses them. He was the human baseline for ImageNet in 2014 and wrote the reproduction of LeCun's 1989 paper on modern hardware.
mentors.ask: If the prompt is the program, who is the programmer?

dialogue.you: Where do I start with models?
dialogue.m: With the smallest one you can write yourself. His course opens with a from-scratch autograd engine and a character-level bigram model before anything larger.
Count which character follows which, then pick the likely next one. Makemore part one builds exactly that from scratch, with training, sampling and a loss.

dialogue.you: Why from scratch when a library exists?
dialogue.m: Because the understanding comes from code you can run. The track goes micrograd, makemore, a WaveNet, a GPT to the 2017 paper, then the tokenizer.

dialogue.you: And for people who only use the models?
dialogue.m: There is a general track next to the technical one on his page: the same ideas, without the mathematics.

exercise.title: A bigram model in twenty lines
steps: Write workspace/mentors/karpathy/bigram.py with TEXT = 'the cat sat on the mat'.
Count every pair of neighbouring characters into a dictionary of dictionaries.
Find the character that most often follows 'a' and print exactly: after a: t
Run it: python3 bigram.py. Then add notes.md with ## What I learned.

mentors.name: Yann LeCun
mentors.role: Turing Award 2018; convolutional networks; Meta AI chief scientist
mentors.bio: Applied backpropagation to handwritten digits in 1989 and invented the convolutional network that read cheques and zip codes in production in the 1990s. Shared the 2018 Turing Award with Hinton and Bengio. Argues loudly for open-weight models and that autoregressive LLMs are not the road to human-level intelligence; his alternative is JEPA, predicting in representation space.
ideas: Open weights let the world inspect and build; closed frontier models concentrate power.
Next-token prediction is a dead end for true understanding; predict abstractions, not pixels or tokens.
Engineering scepticism is healthy: ask what the system actually learns.
mentors.deep: His 2022 position paper lays out a world-model architecture (JEPA) where the system learns to predict the abstract representation of the next state rather than every detail. Whatever one thinks of the forecast, it is the clearest statement of the case that today's LLMs are a plateau, and worth reading against the scaling-law view at Stop 4.
src: A Path Towards Autonomous Machine Intelligence (LeCun 2022, OpenReview)
Backpropagation applied to handwritten zip code recognition (1989)
mentors.ask: He does not think the thing I am using is the future?

dialogue.you: Why is he not impressed by the thing I am using?
dialogue.m: He argues that predicting the next token does not give a system a model of the world: it can sound right, hallucinate, and neither reason nor plan.
Predicting in an abstract representation space instead of predicting every pixel. V-JEPA drops the detail nobody can predict, such as each leaf moving, and keeps what the scene is about.
Because these assistants will sit between people and their knowledge, and he does not think one company should own that layer.
He calls the doom case overstated: intelligence on its own does not produce a will to dominate. Hold that next to what Hinton says and keep both.

exercise.title: What mattered, and what you could throw away
steps: Take one task you gave an agent recently.
Write workspace/mentors/lecun/abstraction.md with ## What mattered and ## What I could throw away.
Under the first, the few facts the answer depended on. Under the second, everything you fed it that turned out to be noise.
Add notes.md with ## What I learned.
exercise.done: abstraction.md separates what mattered from what you could throw away

encounter.plaque: Predict the idea, not the pixel

mentors.name: Geoffrey Hinton
mentors.role: Backpropagation, deep learning; Nobel Prize in Physics 2024
mentors.bio: Co-author of the 1986 paper that made backpropagation practical, teacher of Sutskever and Krizhevsky (AlexNet), Turing Award 2018, Nobel Prize in Physics 2024 for foundational work on learning in neural networks. Left Google in 2023 to speak freely about risks.
ideas: Distributed representations: a concept is a pattern across many units, not one unit.
Learning by error propagation scales; hand-written rules do not.
Take the risks seriously; the people who built it are worried.
mentors.deep: The 1986 Nature paper is three pages and readable. His Nobel lecture and the prize's popular-science summary explain Boltzmann machines and why physics gave the prize. His post-2023 interviews are the clearest lay statement of why some pioneers turned cautious.
mentors.ask: He won a physics prize for this?

dialogue.m: He was one of the researchers who introduced back-propagation, and distributed representations come from that line of work: a concept is a pattern across many units, never one unit.

dialogue.you: And a Nobel Prize in physics?
dialogue.m: Shared with John Hopfield in 2024, for the discoveries that make machine learning with neural networks possible. His Boltzmann machine learns to recognise characteristic elements in data.

dialogue.you: Why does he warn about it now?
dialogue.m: He argued in Cambridge that large scale digital computation is probably far better at acquiring knowledge than biological computation, and may soon be much more intelligent than us.

exercise.title: Twenty steps of learning from error
steps: Write workspace/mentors/hinton/descent.py with w = 0.0 and the target function f(w) = (w - 3) ** 2.
Twenty times: compute the gradient 2 * (w - 3) and take a step of 0.1 against it.
Print each step, and at the end print exactly: w = 3.0 (use round(w, 1)).
Run it: python3 descent.py. Then add notes.md with ## What I learned.

mentors.name: Fei-Fei Li
mentors.bio: Built ImageNet from 2007: 14 million hand-labelled images, when most of the field thought data was a solved problem and algorithms were the bottleneck. The 2012 ImageNet competition result started the deep-learning era. Co-founded Stanford's Institute for Human-Centered AI.
ideas: Data is the bottleneck more often than the algorithm.
Benchmarks change fields: a shared measure makes progress visible.
Keep humans at the centre of the design.
mentors.deep: The story of ImageNet is the story of how a benchmark, not a model, forced everyone to compare honestly. Her memoir The Worlds I See tells it; the ImageNet site still hosts the challenge history. For a chief of staff the transferable lesson is Evening 3 Stop 8: build the measure first.
mentors.ask: So the list of labelled pictures mattered more than the clever maths?

dialogue.m: A shared labelled set at a size nobody had tried: about fourteen million images across roughly twenty-two thousand categories, organised on the WordNet hierarchy.

dialogue.you: So the algorithm was not the hard part?
dialogue.m: The data was, and the fact that everyone could measure on the same set. That is what made progress visible.
Human-centred AI at Stanford: a framework for research, education, practice and policy that starts from human needs rather than from the model.

exercise.title: Label ten things yourself
steps: Pick ten things you can see: files in a folder, emails, photos, tabs.
Write workspace/mentors/li/labels.csv with the header item,label and one row each.
Use only two or three labels, and keep them honest: the hard rows are the lesson.
Add notes.md with ## What I learned, including which row you could not decide.
exercise.done: labels.csv has the item,label header and ten labelled rows

mentors.name: Rich Sutton
mentors.role: Reinforcement learning; the Bitter Lesson; Turing Award 2024
mentors.bio: Co-wrote the standard reinforcement learning textbook, shared the 2024 Turing Award with Andrew Barto, and in 2019 wrote the one-page Bitter Lesson that the Claude Code team keeps on the wall.
ideas: Methods that scale with computation win over methods that encode human knowledge.
The lesson is bitter because it keeps being relearned.
Search and learning are the two general methods.
mentors.deep: The essay is short enough to read at the signpost. The textbook (free online) is the reference for RL, the technique behind RLHF at Stop 5. His argument is the intellectual backbone of the scaling era and of Cherny's "build for the model six months out".

dialogue.m: That general methods which ride on more computation keep beating methods built around what we happen to know, over decades and across fields.
Two: search and learning. Deep Blue searched, AlphaGo Zero learned without the expert knowledge, and vision gave up its hand-made features.
Because it is less flattering to us than researchers expected, so they have been slow to accept it, and keep relearning it.
The 2024 Turing Award with Andrew Barto, for the foundations of reinforcement learning: a machine that learns from experience, which is what Turing asked for in 1947.

exercise.title: The rule you wrote against plain search
steps: Write workspace/mentors/sutton/search.py with NUMS = [2, 17, 30, 41, 55, 70, 88].
First try a rule you invent for finding the two numbers that add up to 100, and print what it gives.
Then try every pair. Print exactly: search found: 30 70
Run it: python3 search.py. Then add notes.md with ## What I learned.

mentors.name: Dario Amodei
mentors.bio: Co-author of the 2020 scaling-laws paper, former VP of research at OpenAI, co-founded Anthropic in 2021 with a safety-first thesis. Wrote Core Views on AI Safety and the essay Machines of Loving Grace on what could go right.
ideas: Scaling is predictable; that is both the opportunity and the reason for caution.
Interpretability and alignment research have to keep pace with capability.
Be honest about uncertainty, in both directions.
mentors.deep: The scaling-laws paper is where the power-law plots come from. Core Views explains why Anthropic trains frontier models at all while worrying about them. Machines of Loving Grace is the optimistic case, written to be argued with. Read both and you understand the company behind the tool you are using.
src: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
mentors.ask: Does the man who runs the company think it is dangerous?

dialogue.you: Why does everyone expect more every year?
dialogue.m: Because the loss follows a power law in model size, dataset size and compute, measured over more than seven orders of magnitude. He is one of the authors of that paper.
Predictable enough that the plan is the easy part, which is exactly why the care is needed.

His company publishes three worlds rather than one: the optimistic, the intermediate where the problem is real but tractable, and the pessimistic. Safety work has to happen at the frontier because large models differ from small ones.
It is stating the uncertainty in both directions instead of picking the convenient end of it.

exercise.title: A forecast you can be wrong about
steps: Write workspace/mentors/amodei/forecast.md with ## What I expect in a year and ## What would change my mind.
Make the first specific enough to be wrong: a number, a date, a task you think will or will not work.
Make the second an observation you could actually make.
Add notes.md with ## What I learned.
sections: ## What I expect in a year
exercise.done: forecast.md carries a falsifiable expectation and what would change your mind

mentors.name: Chris Olah
mentors.bio: Co-founder of Anthropic and of Distill, the journal that made machine learning explanations visual. Leads the work on looking inside models: finding features and circuits that correspond to concepts, including in production Claude models.
ideas: A model is not a black box if you are willing to look.
Features are the units of understanding; circuits are how they combine.
Explain with pictures.
mentors.deep: Transformer Circuits publishes the research: from toy models to finding millions of features in a real Claude model. For Evening 3 the takeaway is that non-determinism and hallucination are being studied mechanically, not just mitigated with rules, and that your checks are the practical layer on top of that science.
mentors.ask: So someone is actually reading its mind?

dialogue.you: Is the model a black box?
dialogue.m: Only if nobody looks. The whole thread asks whether a transformer can be reverse engineered into a program a person can read.
Features, the interpretable units pulled out with sparse autoencoders, and the circuits that connect them into behaviour.
Because an explanation you can see and poke at is the point. Distill was built for that, and for paying down the research debt that builds up when nobody explains.

exercise.title: Draw the circuit of one decision
steps: Pick one decision a tool makes for you: a spam filter, a recommendation, an autocomplete.
Write workspace/mentors/olah/circuit.md with ## What I looked at and your best guess at the inputs, the middle and the output.
Draw it as a mermaid flowchart in a fenced block that starts with three backticks and the word mermaid.
Add notes.md with ## What I learned.
exercise.done: circuit.md holds a mermaid diagram and what you looked at

mentors.name: Mitchell Hashimoto
mentors.role: Creator of Ghostty; co-founder of HashiCorp
mentors.bio: Co-founded HashiCorp (Vagrant, Terraform), then spent his time building Ghostty: a terminal emulator that is fast, native on macOS, and configured with one plain text file. Writes carefully about how he uses AI agents in his own work.
ideas: A tool you use for eight hours a day deserves to be excellent.
Configuration should be one readable file.
Use agents for the parts you understand well enough to review.
mentors.deep: Ghostty's docs are the reference for the terminal setup at Evening 4 Stop 2. His public writing on working with AI is unusually concrete about what he lets agents do and what he does not, which makes it a good counterweight to hype in either direction.
mentors.ask: Why did the Terraform man build a terminal?

dialogue.m: Because you are in it all day. He started Ghostty and libghostty after HashiCorp, where he was on the first engineering team behind Terraform and Vault.
In one file called config.ghostty in your config folder. Plain key = value lines, and a comment is a line that starts with a hash.

dialogue.you: How much do I have to configure?
dialogue.m: Almost nothing. The defaults are meant to be sensible, and every key also works as a command-line flag.

exercise.title: One readable config file
steps: Write workspace/mentors/hashimoto/config.ghostty with at least three key = value lines for a terminal you would actually want.
Above each one, a comment line starting with a hash that says why, not what.
Keys are lowercase; a value can be quoted or bare. Read the docs first.
Add notes.md with ## What I learned.
exercise.done: config.ghostty has three settings and a reason above each

mentors.name: Linus Torvalds
mentors.bio: Wrote git in 2005 in about two weeks after the Linux kernel lost its previous version-control tool. Designed it around content-addressed snapshots and cheap branching, which is why every command at Stops 3 and 4 makes sense once you know that model.
ideas: A commit is a snapshot of everything, named by its hash.
Branches are cheap; use them for every idea.
History is data; rewriting it locally is fine, rewriting it after sharing is rude.
mentors.deep: The official git book is free and the first three chapters are enough for everything in this course. The Pro Git chapter on internals explains the content-addressed model in ten pages; read it once and the commands stop feeling arbitrary.
mentors.ask: Two weeks? For the thing everyone uses?

dialogue.m: A snapshot with a name. Git stores content as objects and names each one by the SHA-1 of a small header plus the content itself.
Of the word blob, a space, the byte count, a zero byte, then the content. The book hashes 'what is up, doc?' and gets bd9dbf5 and the rest.

dialogue.you: Why should that matter to me?
dialogue.m: Because once the name is the content, losing work gets hard. Branches are cheap for the same reason: they are only a name pointing at one of those objects.

exercise.title: Hash a blob the way git does
steps: Write workspace/mentors/torvalds/hash.py using hashlib.
Build the bytes b'blob ' + the length + b'\x00' + b'what is up, doc?' and take the SHA-1 hexdigest.
Print exactly: bd9dbf5aae1a3862dd1526723246b20206e5fc37
Check yourself: echo -n 'what is up, doc?' | git hash-object --stdin. Then add notes.md with ## What I learned.
exercise.done: python3 hash.py prints the same hash as git hash-object

mentors.name: The OpenCode team
mentors.bio: An open-source agent for the terminal that works with Claude, GPT, Gemini and local models, reads AGENTS.md and the Agent Skills standard. Useful as the second opinion that shows which parts of your setup are yours and which belong to the vendor.
ideas: Provider-agnostic by design: swap the model, keep the workflow.
Open source means you can read how the agent decides.
Local models are a first-class option.
mentors.deep: Install it once, run it on the template repo, and compare notes with the Claude Code sessions. The interesting result is not which is better; it is how much of your AGENTS.md and skills carry over unchanged, which is the measure of how portable your setup really is.
mentors.ask: So this one is free and it reads my rules too?

dialogue.m: opencode is an open source coding agent that runs in your terminal, your editor or on the desktop.

dialogue.you: Am I tied to one model?
dialogue.m: No. It reaches more than seventy-five providers through Models.dev, local models included.

dialogue.you: Do I have to rewrite my rules for it?
dialogue.m: It reads AGENTS.md, walking up from the folder you are in, then a global file, and it can fall back to a CLAUDE.md.
MIT, in the open on GitHub, so you can read how the agent decides instead of guessing.

exercise.title: The same prompt, two providers
steps: Write workspace/mentors/opencode/providers.md with ## The same prompt and ## What I would keep.
Under the first, one prompt you use often, written out in full.
Under the second, what stays the same whichever model runs it: your rules file, your checks, your review step.
Add notes.md with ## What I learned.
exercise.done: providers.md holds one prompt and what survives a change of model

encounter.plaque: Swap the model, keep the rules

artifacts.name: The cafe
artifacts.prop: the terrace of the Hospitality Hub
artifacts.what: You are the client, Rolinda is the server, the menu is the protocol. You send a request; she sends a response with a status code and a body. Every API on the internet is this cafe with more tables.
artifacts.rolinda: You asked for a coffee and got a coffee. What did you get when you asked for something that is not on the menu?

real.title: Serve one request and get a 404 on purpose
steps: Write cafe.py. Subclass BaseHTTPRequestHandler as the docs show and answer 200 on the path /coffee and 404 on anything else.
Start it with HTTPServer(('', 8000), Handler) on a background thread, the way the docs' run() function does.
Ask it two questions with http.client: GET /coffee and GET /unicorn-milk.
Print exactly 'GET /coffee -> 200' and then 'GET /unicorn-milk -> 404', then shut the server down.
real.done: cafe.py runs, serves both requests to itself and prints both lines

artifacts.name: The fountain
artifacts.what: The first cup takes a walk to the well. The fountain keeps a copy, so the second cup is instant. A cache is a remembered answer: fast, cheap, and wrong once the world moves on. Claude's prompt cache does the same for the start of your prompt.
artifacts.rolinda: The second cup was instant. How does the fountain know when the water in it is old?

real.title: Put a cache in front of a slow answer
steps: Write fountain.py with a function that sleeps for half a second and returns an answer.
Decorate it with @lru_cache, exactly as the docs write it.
Call it twice with the same argument and time both calls.
Print the two durations and then fountain.cache_info(), which the docs say reports hits, misses, maxsize and currsize.
real.done: cache_info() reports one hit and one miss after two identical calls

artifacts.name: The well
artifacts.what: Pulling a bucket is a query. Without a rope marked in metres you go down the whole well; an index is that rope. Two buckets at once is a transaction: both come up, or neither.
artifacts.rolinda: Why did the second pull take four milliseconds when the first took most of a second?

real.title: A table, an index and one transaction
steps: Write well.py. Connect with sqlite3.connect('well.db') and take a cursor, as the tutorial on that page does.
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS scores, then CREATE TABLE scores(player, score) and insert at least five rows so a rerun always starts clean.
CREATE INDEX scores_player ON scores(player).
Move ten points from one player to another as two UPDATE statements and one con.commit(), then print the rows.
real.done: well.db holds a scores table with rows and an index on player

artifacts.name: The lighthouse
artifacts.what: Ships know the harbour by name; packets need a number. The lighthouse is the resolver: it turns tpetedb.github.io into an address and remembers the answer for a while. It never carries you anywhere.
artifacts.rolinda: The lighthouse pointed at the harbour. Who told the lighthouse where the harbour is?

real.title: Turn a name into an address, twice over
steps: Write lookup.py that calls socket.gethostbyname('localhost'). The docs say it translates a host name to IPv4 address format.
Print 'localhost -> ' and the address you got back. It came from your hosts file, not from the network.

Call socket.getaddrinfo('localhost', 80) and print family.name for every answer, not the family itself: AddressFamily is an IntEnum, and since Python 3.11 printing one gives the bare number. The docs say gethostbyname does not do IPv6 and getaddrinfo should be used instead for a dual stack.

Now look up a name that cannot exist, such as vibe-map.invalid, inside a try block that catches socket.gaierror, and print what happened. Some resolvers answer anyway; knowing that yours does is the lesson.
real.done: it resolves localhost and reports the families getaddrinfo returns

artifacts.name: The dock
artifacts.what: A crate packed here opens the same on every island: the code, its runtime and its libraries in one box. Build packs it, push ships it, run unloads it. That is why it works on the other machine too.
artifacts.rolinda: The crate ran on the other island without a single change. What exactly was in it?

real.title: Write a Dockerfile and build the image
steps: Write app.py: one print statement is enough.
Write a Dockerfile in the order that page uses: FROM python:3.12-slim, WORKDIR /app, COPY . ., CMD.
Build it with the command the docs give, tagging it vibe-dock.
Run it. The output has to be the same as running app.py on your own machine; that is the whole point of the crate.
real.done: a Dockerfile whose instructions all parse, and an image that builds when Docker is installed

artifacts.name: The windmill
artifacts.what: The mill turns without you. A schedule is five fields (minute, hour, day, month, weekday) and a command; a hook is the same command fired by an event instead of a clock. Both are how agents work while you sleep.
artifacts.rolinda: It turned at nine on Monday. What happens if nobody is there to see it fail?

real.title: A workflow that turns without you

doc.title: GitHub Actions docs: Events that trigger workflows

steps: Write nightly.yml with an on: schedule: block and one cron line, in the POSIX cron syntax that page documents.
Give it a job with runs-on: ubuntu-latest and one step that echoes the date.
Read the two warnings on that page: five minutes is the shortest interval, and a scheduled run can be delayed under load.
Copy it to .github/workflows/ in your camp when you want it to run for real.
real.done: nightly.yml parses and has a schedule trigger and a job with steps

artifacts.name: The balloon
artifacts.concept: the cloud, rented by the hour
artifacts.what: The cloud is a computer you rent and never see. The meter runs while the balloon is up, whether you look at it or not; region, size, storage and traffic are four meters, not one. Landing it is the only way to stop paying.
artifacts.rolinda: You rented it for an hour and left it up for a month. Who got the bill?

real.title: Put a number on the meter before you launch
steps: Read that page: you pay by the hour or the second, from launch until you stop or terminate, with no commitment.
Pick one instance type and one region, look its hourly rate up, and write meter.py with that rate and the page you took it from in a comment.
Work out two numbers: the cost of two hours, and the cost of leaving it running for thirty days.
Print '2 hours: <n> USD' and '30 days: <n> USD'. The second one is why you set a budget alarm before the first launch.
real.done: meter.py cites the AWS page it took the rate from and prints both costs

artifacts.name: The mountain
artifacts.what: Hardware at the foot, then the operating system, the runtime, the libraries, your app, and the agent at the summit reading and writing all of it. Every layer stands on the one below; a bug can live on any of them.
artifacts.rolinda: The app said it crashed. Which of the six layers actually did?
links: Python libraries: what they are for

real.title: Name the six layers under your own keystroke
steps: Write layers.py that asks the platform module about this machine: machine(), platform() and python_version().
Print six numbered lines, '1 hardware' through '6 the agent', each with what you found on that layer.
For layer 4 print the version of one library you have installed; for layer 5 print the name of this camp.
Note which of the six the platform module could not tell you. The docs warn that processor() often returns nothing.
real.done: layers.py prints all six layers with real values from this machine

artifacts.name: The market stall
artifacts.what: The menu on the stall is the API: what you may ask for, in which words, and what comes back. Order without reading it and you get a 404 for a wrong path or a 400 for a wrong body. Show your key and you get the good stuff.
artifacts.rolinda: You ordered with the wrong words and got an error. Was that the stall's fault or yours?

real.title: An API with a menu it writes itself
steps: A camp has no pyproject.toml, so make this folder a project first: uv init ., then uv add fastapi. Write main.py with the app from that page, exactly as it stands.
Add a second route, @app.get('/coffee'), that returns a small dictionary.
Run it with uv run fastapi dev and open /docs and /openapi.json in the browser. That menu is generated, never written by hand.
Under a __main__ guard, call your own app with TestClient from fastapi.testclient: GET '/', then print the status code and the body.
real.done: main.py holds the documented app and its test client gets 200 and Hello World

artifacts.name: The bridge
artifacts.what: On the other bank lives a tool the agent does not have. The bridge has a rulebook: first ask what is over there, then call it by name with the arguments it expects. That rulebook is MCP, and every connector is one more bridge.
artifacts.rolinda: The agent found three tools on the other side. Who decides which of them it may use?

real.title: Declare one server on the other side

doc.title: MCP docs: Build an MCP server

steps: Read the configuration block on that page: an mcpServers object, one key per server, each with a command and its args.
Write mcp.json here with one server of your own, named for what it does, with an absolute path in args as the page insists.
Heed the warning on that page: the command may need the full path to the executable, which you get from which uv.
Copy the block into .mcp.json at the root of your camp, then ask your agent to list its tools.
real.done: mcp.json is valid JSON and lists at least one server with a command

artifacts.name: The factory
artifacts.what: Raw is what arrived, bronze keeps it as it came, silver cleans and types it, gold answers one question; each step reads the one before and writes its own table. A good pipeline is idempotent: a failed run leaves nothing half-written, and a rerun on the same input gives the same output with no duplicates.
artifacts.rolinda: Run 41 fell over halfway through. Why did the gold numbers not change, and why was that the right thing?

real.title: Raw to bronze to silver to gold, in one file
steps: Write raw.csv by hand: played_at, player, score, and six rows, one of them with a score that is not a number.
Write pipeline.py. Connect with duckdb.connect('camp.duckdb'), the persistent form that page shows.
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE bronze AS SELECT * FROM read_csv('raw.csv', all_varchar = true): bronze keeps what arrived.
Make silver by casting score to an integer and dropping the row that will not cast, then make gold: one row per player with their best score. Print the row count of each.
real.done: camp.duckdb holds a gold table with rows in it

artifacts.name: The post office
artifacts.prop: the post office on the south point
artifacts.what: You drop a letter and walk away; the queue keeps it until every subscriber has read it, even one that was offline. Delivery is at least once, so a reader must cope with the same letter twice, and a letter nobody can read goes to the dead-letter shelf instead of being retried forever.
artifacts.rolinda: The vault writer was offline for twenty minutes and still got the letter. Who kept it, and what if it arrives twice?

real.title: A queue, a retry and a dead letter
steps: Write postoffice.py with the worker from that page: a queue.Queue, a daemon thread that loops on q.get(), and q.task_done() after each item.
Put three letters in. The docs say a FIFO queue hands back the first task added first, so the order is yours to predict.
Make letter 3 fail once. Put it back with its attempt count and print 'retry 3' when the worker picks it up again.
Make it fail a second time and print 'dead letter 3' instead of retrying forever. Finish with q.join() and print the whole order: delivered 1, delivered 2, retry 3, dead letter 3.
real.done: the output shows both deliveries, one retry and one dead letter, in that order

artifacts.name: The switchboard
artifacts.prop: the switchboard by the fourth plot
artifacts.what: An operator's panel: every line on the campus ends in a labelled socket, and you connect one by name instead of remembering which wire went where. A justfile is that panel for a project. Each task is a recipe with a name and a comment above it, just --list reads the labels back to you, and the same recipe is what a git hook, a CI job and your agent run, so there is one wire per job and nobody patches by hand.
artifacts.rolinda: Everyone here runs the tests a slightly different way. Which of those ways is the one the pipeline runs?

real.title: Write a justfile with three recipes and let your agent run one
steps: Write a justfile in this folder with three recipes, and put a comment on the line directly above each one: the Documentation Comments chapter says that comment is what just --list prints next to the recipe.
Give one recipe a parameter with a default, the way Recipe Parameters shows (greet name='camp':), and give one recipe a dependency by naming another recipe after its colon.
Run just --list, then run each recipe, then just --dump --dump-format json to see your own tasks as data. That JSON is what the check reads.

Let your agent run one. Add the allow rule Bash(just *) to .claude/settings.json (the permissions page puts the wildcard after the program, so this covers your recipes and nothing else) and ask it to run a recipe by name.
real.done: the justfile parses, has three recipes, every one documented, one with a parameter and one with a dependency

artifacts.name: The shop
artifacts.prop: the shop on the main street
artifacts.what: uv add polars is a purchase: the shelf is PyPI, every version sits on it with a date, and the wish goes into pyproject.toml. The receipt is uv.lock, exact versions and checksums, so uv sync --frozen rebuilds the same environment on any machine; a yanked version stays on the shelf with a warning not to take it.
artifacts.rolinda: You bought polars once and it works on CI too. Which file is the receipt, and what happens if you delete it?
links: Python libraries: what they are for

real.title: Buy a library and keep the receipt
steps: In this folder run uv init . as that guide does, which writes pyproject.toml.
Run uv add humanize. The wish goes into pyproject.toml; the exact version goes into uv.lock.
Open both files and find humanize in each. The guide calls uv.lock a cross-platform lockfile with the exact resolved versions, and says to check it into version control.
Run uv run python -c "import humanize; print(humanize.naturalsize(1024))" and watch it work without you activating anything.
real.done: pyproject.toml asks for humanize and uv.lock records the version it resolved to

artifacts.name: The bank
artifacts.what: A token is a key: whoever holds it is you, as far as the server can tell. It lives in .env or the keychain, never in a commit and never in a vault note; a leaked key is revoked the minute you know, and rotating keys on a schedule means a leak you did not notice dies on its own.
artifacts.rolinda: The key ended up in a public gist at nine. What did you do at one minute past, and why not go looking for the leak first?

real.title: A safe, and the note that says what is in it
steps: Write .gitignore here with one line: .env. That page explains why a pattern without a slash matches the file at any level below.
Write .env with one fake key, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-not-a-real-key. It never leaves your machine.
Write env.example with the same name and nothing after the equals sign. The repository holds the names, never the values.
Run git check-ignore -v .env and read which rule caught it; the page explains the precedence it printed.
real.done: .gitignore ignores .env and env.example names the key without a value

artifacts.name: The data centre
artifacts.prop: the hall next to the Hub
artifacts.what: A request travels to the nearest edge, waits for a GPU node, reads your prompt in one pass and then types the answer one token at a time; most of the wait is the typing. Distance adds latency, a node that has to load the weights first adds a cold start, and batch jobs fill the GPUs cheaply because nobody is waiting.
artifacts.rolinda: The same question took two seconds from Amsterdam and forty from a node that had just woken up. Which part of the building was slow?
links: Open weights versus closed models, on your own Mac

real.title: The same work, one at a time and in a batch
steps: Write batch.py with a function that sleeps for a tenth of a second and returns; that stands for a request waiting on a GPU somewhere.
Call it twenty times in a plain loop and time it.
Call it twenty times again inside a ThreadPoolExecutor, with the submit and as_completed pattern that page shows.
Print 'one at a time: <n> s', 'batched: <n> s' and 'speedup: <n>x'. The room was never faster; it was just no longer half empty.
real.done: batch.py reports both timings and the speedup

artifacts.name: The energy grid
artifacts.prop: the pylon and the turbine by the harbour
artifacts.what: Tokens are the watts: every request draws some in and some out, output costs more because it is generated, and the bill is the meter reading times the price per million. A rate limit is a fuse that trips before the wiring melts, autoscaling adds turbines when demand spikes, and a budget alarm rings before the invoice does.
artifacts.rolinda: Request sixty-one came back with a 429 and a Retry-After. Was that the grid failing you, or protecting you?
links: Scaling laws and the Bitter Lesson

real.title: Back off the way the docs tell you to
steps: Read that page: over the limit you get a 429 describing which limit you hit, with a retry-after header saying how many seconds to wait, and earlier retries fail.
Write backoff.py with a stand-in endpoint that returns 429 with retry-after 2, then 429 with no header, then 200.
Write the client loop: honour retry-after when it is there, otherwise double your own wait, starting at two seconds.
Print the schedule rather than sleeping it: '429 retry-after 2', 'waiting 2 s', '429 no retry-after', 'waiting 4 s', '200 OK'.
real.done: the printed schedule honours the header first and doubles when it is absent

artifacts.name: The library
artifacts.what: A question becomes a vector, a long list of numbers, and the notes that sit nearest to it in that space come back as the shelves to read; the model answers from those pages and cites them. The index is a snapshot: a note edited after the last build is invisible until you re-index, so the rebuild belongs on a hook.
artifacts.rolinda: You asked what changed tonight and got yesterday's note with a confident citation. What was out of date, the model or the shelves?
links: Memory: the vault as long-term memory

real.title: Retrieve three notes and cite the one you used
steps: Write retrieve.py. Turn each of four short notes into a Counter of its words; that vector of counts is the crude ancestor of an embedding.
Turn the question into a Counter the same way.
Score every note against the question with cosine similarity: the dot product over the product of the two lengths, with math.sqrt.
Print 'top 3 for: <the question>', then the three best notes with their scores, then an answer line ending in 'source: <the note you used>'.
real.done: retrieve.py ranks the notes and names the one its answer came from

artifacts.name: The office
artifacts.prop: the office tower next to the Hub
artifacts.what: One brief, three roles: a planner reads AGENTS.md and writes the steps, a worker edits and runs the tests, a reviewer reads the diff against the plan and the handbook and may say no. Subagents are departments, each with a fresh context and a narrow brief, reporting back in a paragraph so the main agent's context stays small.
artifacts.rolinda: The reviewer rejected the change because the handbook said never rewrite the scores. Who wrote that rule, and what if nobody had?

real.title: Hire one subagent with a narrow brief

doc.title: Claude Code docs: Create Custom Subagents

steps: Write reviewer.md with the frontmatter that page documents: name in lowercase with hyphens, and a description saying when to use it.
Add a tools line with the read-only tools only. The page says a subagent inherits everything when you leave it out, which is the opposite of a narrow brief.
Write the body: what it reads, what it refuses, and what it reports back, in a few sentences.
Copy it to .claude/agents/ in your camp and ask your agent to use it on a real diff.
real.done: reviewer.md has valid frontmatter with a name and a description

artifacts.name: The households
artifacts.prop: the row of houses on the west shore
artifacts.what: Every row in a users table is a person and every column is something of theirs, held with their consent for a stated purpose. Collect only what the feature needs, share aggregates and hashes rather than rows, and design the delete before the insert, because a request to see or erase everything you hold must be answered within thirty days.
artifacts.rolinda: The leaderboard shows a name and a score. Why does it also have their birthday in the table, and who asked for it?

real.title: Export one person's rows, then erase them
steps: Write erase.py that writes players.csv from a small list at the top of the file with csv.DictWriter, so every run starts from the same data.
Read it back with csv.DictReader and split the rows in two: the ones belonging to one person, and the rest.
Write that person's rows to export.csv: that is the access request answered.
Write the rest back over players.csv: that is the erasure. Print 'exported <n> rows' and 'erased <n> rows'.
real.done: erase.py exports the person's rows and rewrites players.csv without them

artifacts.name: The school
artifacts.what: Data goes in, weights come out: the model is a very long list of numbers adjusted a little on every example until the loss stops falling. The data is split once into train and test, the exam the model never sees while learning, so a train score far above the test score means it memorised the homework; a benchmark is that exam shared by every model, one number that can be compared.
artifacts.rolinda: Ninety-nine percent on the homework and seventy-one on the exam. Which of those two numbers would you put on a slide, and why is that the wrong instinct?
links: Evals: measure the agent, not the vibe

real.title: Split the data, train, and read the honest number
steps: A camp has no pyproject.toml, so make this folder a project first: uv init ., then uv add scikit-learn. Write split.py.
Build a small table of your own: a few hundred rows with two numbers and a label that mostly follows them.
Split it with train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.33, random_state=42), the call that page gives, so the split is the same every run.
Fit a DecisionTreeClassifier, then print 'train accuracy: <n>' and 'test accuracy: <n>'. Raise max_depth until the two numbers part company: that gap is the overfit.
real.done: split.py splits with a fixed random_state and reports both scores
